extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of propaganda/media studies, journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Identify, describe, and evaluate instances and techniques of atrocity propaganda — information (often fabricated or exaggerated) used to portray an enemy as monstrously criminal in order to sway opinion or justify violence. Useful for historical analysis, media literacy, and detecting misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: spreading information about enemy crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Atrocity propaganda is the spreading of information about the crimes committed by an enemy, which can be factual, but often includes or features deliberate fabrications or exaggerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers a range of media (photographs, videos, illustrations, interviews, and other forms of reporting). Useful diagnostic: check whether reports are corroborated or appear to be embellished or fabricated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabrication or exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Often includes or features deliberate fabrications or exaggerations of alleged crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the article include invented atrocity stories from World War I (mutilated babies, crucified soldiers, 'corpse factories'), the Nayirah testimony, and fabricated eyewitness accounts. Anti-pattern: accepting lurid claims without independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and formats employed
rubrics_metrics.description: Atrocity propaganda can involve photographs, videos, illustrations, interviews, lurid newspaper stories, propaganda films, and fabricated official reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form is part of its persuasive power — sensational images and witness statements are commonly used to attract reprinting and public attention. Verify provenance of images and witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a baseline lie
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagandists often establish a baseline lie and then paint the enemy as a monster around that lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This baseline lie functions as a foundation that subsequent stories build upon; investigators should trace back to the earliest source and check for independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonization / dehumanization of the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Atrocity propaganda seeks to make the enemy appear savage, barbaric, inhumane, or subhuman to arouse hatred and justify harsh measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include emotionally charged language, stereotypical portrayals (e.g. 'subhuman'), and framing that strips opponents of moral status. Look for language that denies group humanity or moral complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive tone: violent, gloomy, doom-laden messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The messaging is violent, gloomy, and portrays doom to rile up and excite the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories emphasise horror, imminent threat, and moral outrage (e.g. rape tales, mutilations, massacres). Check whether reporting prioritizes shock value over verifiable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting audiences including officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagandists aim to influence perceptions, attitudes, opinions, and policies, often targeting officials at all levels of government as well as the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns may be designed to sway policymakers (to create a casus belli) as well as to mobilize public support; examine intended audiences and channels used (press, congressional testimony, diplomatic briefings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated or staged testimony / witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: False or staged eyewitness testimony is a recurrent technique (e.g., Nayirah’s congressional testimony; fabricated photographer accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify witness identity, affiliation, and independence. Beware testimony that is amplified by PR firms or state actors without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational recurring themes (children, sexual violence, mutilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain themes — attacks on children, sexual violence (rapes), crucifixion-like tortures, mutilations — are repeatedly used because they provoke visceral public reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These themes are highly persuasive but also commonly fabricated or exaggerated; such claims demand especially rigorous verification and corroboration from neutral sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured 'official' reports and committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Propagandists sometimes produce or exploit official-sounding reports (committees, inquiries, published reports) to lend legitimacy to atrocity claims, even when evidence is weak or files are missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Bryce Report in WWI — investigators should inspect methodology, source files, and whether original documentation is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press amplification and commercial incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and media outlets may reprint sensational atrocity stories (sometimes fabricated) for circulation and influence (yellow journalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that commercial motives (e.g., Pulitzer/Hearst era examples) and media competition can drive acceptance and spread of false atrocity narratives; cross-check with multiple independent outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaponizing falsehoods to influence neutrals and mislead the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsehoods are used deliberately to deceive one's own people, attract neutrals, and mislead the enemy (including as an intelligence function to waste enemy resources).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda may be strategically timed and aimed; analyze intended strategic effect, not just factual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backfire effects: causing mistrust or incitement to real atrocities
rubrics_metrics.description: Atrocity propaganda can have secondary harms: it may incite further violence by the other side or one's own side, and it can cause the public to mistrust genuine reports of atrocities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to both immediate mobilizing effects and longer-term credibility loss; historical examples include postwar skepticism about later true reports because earlier tales were debunked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in peacetime or pretext creation (casus belli)
rubrics_metrics.description: Atrocity propaganda is not limited to wartime; it may be implemented to sway public opinion or create a casus belli to justify initiating war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize dramatic atrocity allegations that precede calls for military action; examine whether they originated in adversary/state actors seeking policy goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denying/labeling true reports as propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors accused of real crimes sometimes dismiss credible reports as 'atrocity propaganda' to discredit victims and delay accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine evidence-based rebuttals and blanket denials that rely on the prior delegitimization of sources or the concept of 'it’s propaganda' without counter-evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability problems with human testimony in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: Human testimony can be unreliable in ordinary circumstances and more so in wartime due to bias, sentiment, and patriotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat uncorroborated eyewitness accounts with caution; corroborate through multiple independent sources, material evidence, or contemporaneous records.
